message.content:
Here’s a quick snapshot of some of the most celebrated American composers—across genres and eras—who have left an indelible mark on music worldwide:

| Composer | Era / Style | Notable Works / Contributions |
|----------|-------------|--------------------------------|
| **John Philip Sousa** (1854‑1932) | Late Romantic / Military Marches | “The Stars and Stripes Forever,” “Washington Post March” – the quintessential American march composer. |
| **Scott Joplin** (1868‑1917) | Ragtime | “Maple Leaf Rag,” “The Entertainer” – the “King of Ragtime.” |
| **George Gershwin** (1898‑1937) | Jazz‑Classical Fusion | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris,” Broadway hits like “Porgy & Bess.” |
| **Aaron Copland** (1900‑1990) | 20th‑Century Classical | “Appalachian Spring,” “Fanfare for the Common Man,” “El Salón México.” |
| **Leonard Bernstein** (1918‑1990) | Broadway & Classical | “West Side Story,” “Candide,” “On the Town” – a bridge between popular and concert music. |
| **Philip Glass** (born 1937) | Minimalism | “Einstein on the Beach,” “Glassworks,” film scores for *The Hours* and *Koyaanisqatsi*. |
| **John Williams** (born 1942) | Film Scores | “Star Wars,” “Indiana Jones,” “Jurassic Park,” “Harry Potter” – arguably the most iconic film composer of all time. |
| **Samuel Barber** (1910‑1981) | 20th‑Century Classical | “Adagio for Strings,” “Knoxville: Summer of 1915.” |
| **William Grant Still** (1895‑1978) | African‑American Classical | “Afro-American Symphony,” “Bluebird of Happiness.” |
| **Charles Ives** (1874‑1954) | Experimental/Modernist | “The Unanswered Question,” “Central Park in the Dark.” |
| **George Gershwin** (1898‑1937) | Jazz‑Classical Fusion | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris.” |
| **John Adams** (born 1947) | Contemporary Classical | “Nixon in China,” “Short Ride in a Fast Machine.” |
| **Steve Reich** (born 1936) | Minimalism | “Music for 18 Musicians,” “Different Trains.” |
| **John Cage** (1912‑1992) | Avant‑Garde | “4′33″,” prepared piano works. |

### Why These Names Stand Out

- **Cultural Impact**: Many of these composers helped define what “American music” sounds like—whether through jazz-infused symphonies, patriotic marches, or groundbreaking film scores.
- **Innovation**: Figures like Ives, Cage, and Reich pushed the boundaries of tonality, rhythm, and performance practice.
- **Cross‑Genre Influence**: Gershwin, Bernstein, and Williams show how classical training can translate into popular and cinematic contexts.

If you’re looking for a deeper dive into any particular composer or era, let me know!
